clue.text: The English way? Ah, no! But a foreign sort

definitions.text: The English way? Ah, no! But a foreign sort

indicators.note: a foreign sort of the letters asks for them to be rearranged into a strange new order

parts.note: the eight letters of these three words supply the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a road is the English kind, and is told no, it belongs abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of AHNOBUTA, signalled by 'foreign sort', gives the answer, and the whole clue also describes it: not an English motorway but a German one.
explanation.definitionFit: A German motorway is the foreign counterpart of the English trunk road, so the whole clue serves as a description.

definitions.meaning: dull and lifeless, as in a performance that falls short
in theatre, a painted wooden screen forming part of the stage set

explanation.definitionFit: Dull describes something lacking interest, and a theatre set is built from painted framed panels of that name.

indicators.note: propagating plants means producing new ones, suggesting the letters of the word are bred into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A gardener earns money by growing cuttings of a flowering sage plant.
explanation.walkthrough: Salvia is a garden plant, so 'propagating' fits a gardening picture, but it is the anagram signal for SALVIA.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to avail is to benefit or be of use, so 'profits' in the sense of 'benefits' is a synonym.

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, shown by the letter O
to dole out is to hand out in portions, so a dole is an allotted share or allowance

explanation.surface: A formal address drawn from the title of the 1930s novel about unemployment, Love on the Dole.
explanation.walkthrough: Love on the Dole is Walter Greenwood's 1933 novel of the Depression; the clue reads it as O placed on (before) a portion handed out.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal public address is a type of speech, so the two words are close synonyms.

parts.note: reads like an attacking rush, but means the fee paid on the way in to an event or venue

explanation.definitionFit: The fee for admission is what you pay as you come in, so it is literally a charge for coming in.

clue.text: Supporters with lots of hard facts

parts.note: brassieres support the bust, so supporters stand for undergarments of that kind
stacks, informally, means a great quantity, as in stacks of money

explanation.surface: Fans armed with plenty of cold, solid evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporters' suggests fans, but it means bras; 'with' simply joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To get down to the basic realities is an idiom built on this phrase, so it means the essential facts.

definitions.meaning: literally a rotten item of food, unpleasant to eat or smell
a rogue or worthless person, the informal sense of the same phrase

explanation.definitionFit: A rotten egg is literally unsavoury, and the phrase is an idiom for a rogue or rascal.

parts.note: reads as a passenger who reserved a ticket quickly, but means a voyager put in a book by Jonathan Swift

explanation.definitionFit: The hero of Jonathan Swift's satire voyages to Lilliput and elsewhere, a traveller in a book by Swift.

clue.text: Usual pattern followed by an Anglo-Saxon conqueror

indicators.note: followed by places the second piece after the first in the answer

parts.note: a norm is the standard or usual pattern of behaviour

explanation.surface: A routine is succeeded by an invader from 1066.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anglo-Saxon conqueror' means one who conquered the Anglo-Saxons, as William's followers did in 1066, not an Anglo-Saxon who conquered.
explanation.definitionFit: The invaders from northern France who defeated Harold in 1066 overcame the Anglo-Saxon kingdom of England.

parts.note: suggests someone gunned down as a safety measure, but means a sliding bar pushed across to fasten a door

explanation.definitionFit: A sliding door fastener is 'shot' home into its socket to keep a room locked and secure.

definitions.meaning: involved or caring about something, as in the parties concerned
having a stake or a personal benefit in the outcome

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both having concern or curiosity and having a personal stake, as in an interested party.

indicators.note: read as out + right: R, the abbreviation for right, goes out of the word

parts.note: a gaffer is a foreman or boss, so foremen are bosses of that name; the 's adds no letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'outright' looks like an adjective meaning complete, but splits as 'out R': take R from GAFFERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Social or diplomatic blunders are a familiar synonym for embarrassing mistakes.

clue.text: Timorous person, eager to acquire the skill

indicators.note: to acquire tells us the eager word takes on the following pieces after it

parts.note: fain is an archaic word for glad or eager
art is a skill, as in the art of conversation

explanation.surface: A nervous type who is keen to learn a craft.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic word for willing is the less obvious synonym; 'to acquire' only signals that the other pieces are attached after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowardly or timid person is called this, from the proverb that it never won fair lady.

parts.note: an event called off is off
a stage or stagecoach is a horse-drawn coach

explanation.surface: Someone is idle because the bus they meant to catch was scrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coach' suggests a modern bus or a sports trainer, but here it is the old stagecoach, STAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor out of view in the wings is not currently on stage performing in the play.

definitions.meaning: lets out a rope or line by turning it off a reel
calms down after tension, as after a hard day

explanation.definitionFit: To reel out a cable and to calm down after stress are both senses of the same verb.

clue.text: In poor health, expired taking the waters

indicators.note: taking means the word for expired takes in, or holds, the other piece

parts.note: to expire is to die
the seas are the waters of the world

explanation.surface: A sick person died while visiting a spa for a cure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking the waters' suggests a spa cure, so the surface hides the container: 'taking' means one piece holds the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Sick or affected by illness, so a synonym for being in poor health.

indicators.note: new signals that these letters are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: Asks whether a recruit is a raw cadet or a veteran.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' seems to describe the cadet, but it is the anagram signal for CADETOR.
explanation.definitionFit: British infantrymen of past centuries wore scarlet tunics and were nicknamed for them.

clue.text: Flair shown when skill is added to effort

indicators.note: added to places the following piece on the end of what comes before

parts.note: art is skill, as in the art of fencing
a try is an attempt or effort

explanation.surface: Talent appears when ability is combined with hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces run in clue order: ART, then IS, then TRY tacked on.
explanation.definitionFit: Creative skill and flair are both words for a gifted, artistic touch.

indicators.note: in shows the frolic word placed inside the springtime word

parts.note: May is a month of spring
a lark is a bit of fun or a frolic

explanation.surface: Romping about in spring? What rubbish!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frolic in springtime' reads as one picture, but it is LARK put in MAY. This is a less common spelling, usually MALARKEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Malarkey is informal for meaningless talk, an exclamation of disbelief.

indicators.note: could be suggests these letters might form a different word when rearranged

explanation.surface: This waters might belong to somebody else as a place to fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could be' signals an anagram of ANOTHERS, including the S of the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: The sea between Britain and Scandinavia is a major area for commercial fishing.

clue.text: How a witness may appear to Noah in new guise

indicators.note: in new guise means the letters appear in a new form or disguise

explanation.surface: A witness turns up before Noah dressed differently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in new guise' turns TONOAH into the answer; 'to Noah' is the fodder, not part of the picture of a witness.
explanation.definitionFit: Witnesses in court give evidence under a sworn promise to tell the truth.

parts.note: suggests a U-boat, but means the German word for a substitute

explanation.definitionFit: The German word for replacement is used in English for an inferior imitation or substitute.

indicators.note: changes signals that the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' looks like a noun in the surface, but it is the anagram signal for INLATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To necessitate or involve something as a consequence is a standard meaning of this verb.

indicators.note: from means the answer is made out of these letters, shaped from them as raw material

explanation.surface: Something quite unlike the eastern London district of Poplar.
explanation.walkthrough: Poplar is a district of East London; the answer is made out of the letters of EASTPOPLAR rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning widely separated, like the two ends of the earth, hence entirely unlike.

definitions.meaning: a small amount, as in a little milk in tea
flair or panache, as in cutting a fine figure

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a small added amount and stylish verve or panache.

indicators.note: in shows the king letter sits inside the word for appropriate

parts.note: due means fitting or appropriate, as in due respect
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: An aristocrat with a king in a fitting setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setting' just completes the container idea of K placed in DUE.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest rank of the British peerage below royalty, so a nobleman.

parts.note: suggests tying securely, but means to force someone to go without food

explanation.definitionFit: To deprive of food is to make someone fast, in the sense of going without meals.

parts.note: sounds like the lowest gear of a car, but means clothing worn on the bottom

explanation.definitionFit: Women's underpants, in British usage, are clothing worn over the backside.
